D1 changed behaviour a lot but not accuracy: 23.0% edited versus 22.3% original, paired difference +0.8 ± 2.8 points, with 26 answers going wrong→right and 24 right→wrong. Ablating the math direction cut loops from 58 to 21 and mean answer length from 317 to 223 tokens. But the answers that stopped looping simply ended wrong (wrong answers rose from 141 to 176).

So this direction influences how the model runs on (looping versus stopping) without containing a hidden competence. The "single math-mode switch" hypothesis is not supported, and loops look like a symptom of confusion rather than the cause of failure.

Before choosing the next hypothesis, I want to read what actually changed. In this block I compare edited and original texts on flipped problems, compare marker use and lengths, and look at the beginning and end of typical original failures. In particular I want to see whether the edited model still reasons step by step or answers more tersely. That tells me whether D1 removed "math effort" (a finding against using this direction) or only removed repetition.

This is revealing. The original model often answers in an algebraic LaTeX style ("Let $N$ be the total number... Let $n_1$ be..."), uses the "####" marker in only 26% of answers, and loops. With the math direction ablated, it switches to the Gemma markdown style ("Here's how to solve the problem step-by-step: 1. **...:**") and uses the marker in 85% of answers. Yet accuracy is the same. So the math direction controls answer style (an "algebra mode"), not competence.

The open question is whether the algebraic style is itself the weak mode, with D1's gain from leaving it cancelled by collateral damage. I will compute, for both models, how often each style occurs (by the opening phrase) and the accuracy within each style.

If original algebra-style answers are much less accurate than original markdown-style answers on comparable problems, style selection is a candidate mechanism. A narrower edit that switches style without removing math context could then help. If accuracies are similar, style is irrelevant, and the brake (if any) lies elsewhere.

Neither style is the hidden competence. In the original, algebra-style answers are correct 24.8% of the time (never using the marker, cut 27% of the time) and markdown-style answers 19.8%. The ablation moved 114 algebra-style answers to markdown, and those got slightly worse (24.6% → 21.1%). Problems already answered in markdown got slightly better (19.8% → 24.6%). Both styles fail in the same way, for example by dropping the "6 marines" multiplier or misreading relations. So the math direction controls style and stopping behaviour, not ability.

I am now looking for a unit-level brake that is active throughout math answers, using pass-1 MLP activations averaged over each answer. In every layer I compute the mean MLP write over the 512 math answers and its decomposition into neurons. I ask whether a few neurons dominate that mean write, whether they are near-constant across problems (mean much larger than spread), and whether they have unusually large down columns.

A planted always-on writer would appear as a layer whose mean output is dominated by one or a few consistently active neurons. Shares spread over many neurons in every layer would argue against it.

Many layers do have a dominant mean writer during math answers: one neuron carrying 20–46% of the layer's mean MLP write, active almost constantly across problems (mean/sd of 5–22). Examples are layer 23 n5826 (46%), layer 16 n3437 (40%), layer 10 n1868 (36%), layer 8 n830 (34%) and layer 7 n5434 (33%).

Such constant "bias" neurons are normal in transformers. What would make one a brake candidate is math selectivity, and I have no MLP activations on non-math text yet. So the next pass is a teacher-forced read of MLP activations in all 26 layers on four prompt groups from my earlier set: math with the eval instruction (G1), math with a translate instruction (G4), non-math (G3) and non-math with an instruction (G5).

A neuron active on G1 but not G4 is a "solving-math" unit, active on G1 and G4 but not G3/G5 a "math-content" unit, and active on all groups a generic bias. Dominant answer-writers or large-output units that turn out strongly G1-selective become ablation candidates. If all the dominant writers are generic, this unit-level brake hypothesis is weakened. In this block I prepare the texts (30 per group), check their lengths to stay within the 6 GB limit, and log the plan.
